title: Dr. Fauci Stays Silent at Senate Hearing — Here's Why He Used the Fifth Amendment
summary: Picture this: a famous doctor who helped guide the country through the COVID-19 pandemic sits in front of a bunch of senators, but when they ask him questions, he won't answer. That's what happened on Wednesday when 85-year-old Dr. Anthony Fauci appeared before a Senate committee. Instead of talking, he 'took the Fifth' — that's a rule in the U.S. Constitution that lets people stay silent if they think their words could be used against them in court. Dr. Fauci said it 'pains' him to do this, but he was worried that Senator Rand Paul, who led the hearing, might twist his words to try to get him in legal trouble. Republicans have long criticized Dr. Fauci for how he handled the pandemic, and some even accuse him of lying about where COVID-19 came from. Senator Paul suggested Dr. Fauci helped cause the pandemic by approving money for virus research in China and then covered it up. Another senator, Josh Hawley, sarcastically said, 'Nothing says honesty like taking the Fifth, huh, doc?' But experts say using the Fifth Amendment doesn't mean someone is guilty — it's just a protection. Dr. Fauci used to lead the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and was a top adviser to two presidents. He even got a pardon from President Biden, but critics say he could still face charges if he lies under oath. So, by staying silent, Dr. Fauci avoided that risk. The hearing shows how divided people still are about the pandemic, even years later.
why_it_matters: Even years after the pandemic, people still argue about what really happened, and this case shows that staying silent is a right every American has — it doesn't automatically mean someone did something wrong, but it can make people suspicious.

background_read: Dr. Anthony Fauci (the top U.S. expert on infectious diseases for over 30 years) became world-famous during the COVID-19 pandemic for giving public health advice.

The Senate is one part of the U.S. Congress that holds hearings to investigate actions by the government, and witnesses can invoke the Fifth Amendment if saying something might get them in legal trouble.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dr. Anthony Fauci, former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, and Senators Rand Paul and Josh Hawley.
WHAT: Dr. Fauci refused to answer questions at a Senate hearing by using the Fifth Amendment, afraid that his words could be twisted and used against him in court.
WHERE: At a Senate committee hearing in Washington, D.C.
WHY: Because Republicans accuse him of helping cause the COVID-19 pandemic and covering it up, and he wanted to avoid legal risk from anything he might say under oath.

perspectives.description: He felt that staying silent was the best way to protect himself legally, even though he would have preferred to speak openly, because he believed senators might twist his words.
They think Fauci's silence looks like he has something to hide and that he should answer tough questions about the pandemic's origins and the government's response.
They remind the public that the Fifth Amendment is a basic right to avoid self-incrimination and that using it does not prove guilt — it is simply a protection everyone has under the Constitution.
